notes: Code is identical to C2's complete fix; tests cover dispenser and parser cases plus an unclosed-block error, but lack an adapt test and only loosely check the argument values inside the block.

Production code is identical to C1 and fixes the root cause everywhere braces are structurally checked; its dispenser and parse tests cover quoted open/close braces, nested blocks and an unclosed-block error, but it has no adapt-level test of the issue's exact Caddyfile.

Fixes the core dispenser and parser brace checks, but misses ArgErr and the doImport anonymous-block check, so a quoted "{" there is still treated as structural; good parse, dispenser and adapt tests.

Fixes the main parsing paths and passes the tests, but misses ArgErr and the doImport anonymous-block check, so a quoted "{" can still produce a misleading error or be rejected as an anonymous block; its tests are reasonable, including an adapt test for the issue case.
Same complete fix as C2, written idiomatically with Quoted(); its dedicated table test covers backticks, heredoc, nested blocks, snippet import and the case where a quoted "}" fails to close a block.

Same complete fix as C1/C2, using the existing Quoted() accessor, plus a strong segment-verifying parse test covering backticks, heredocs, nested blocks, snippet import and a quoted brace failing to close a block.

Matches the reference nearly everywhere, including ArgErr and the doImport anonymous-block check; it only skips the minor address HasSuffix tweak, and its parse, dispenser and multi-case integration tests are thorough.

Code matches the reference in substance: it adds token-level unquoted brace helpers and uses them across the dispenser (including ArgErr), import handling, directive parsing and blockTokens; it only skips the quoted HasSuffix address check, the quoted "{}" reordering and the doc-comment updates, and its tests (dispenser, parse cases with an error case, integration adapt test) are thorough.

Essentially the same as C2 (a map of slices with ConfigResource-level parent override), so it fixes the reported case but still silently drops child imports for distinct instances; it has only a single basic for_each test.

Fixes the single-module case by keeping all blocks per ConfigResource, but a parent import still silently drops every child-module import block for that resource, including ones targeting different instances, so the same silent-drop bug survives across modules.

Fixes the reported bug by keeping all blocks, and handles parent-overrides-child per instance through static key comparison; but it assumes overlap whenever a key is dynamic, has a for_each, or carries a module instance key, so it can still silently drop valid child imports that the reference keeps by deduplicating at expansion time.

Comes closest to instance-level overriding by statically comparing instance keys, but it treats dynamic targets (for_each imports, module instance keys) as overlapping and drops child blocks there, which re-parses addresses heuristically where the reference simply dedups after expansion.

Keeps all same-module blocks, which fixes the reported case, but any parent import for a resource still discards every child import of that resource, even for other instances, recreating the same silent-drop bug across modules; its tests cover for_each, count, mixed and child-module cases but never parent/child overlap.

Same logic as C1, with parent blocks overriding all child blocks for the same ConfigResource regardless of instance; it has broader tests (for_each, count, mixed, child module) but none for parent/child override with distinct instances.

Returns a slice like the reference and keeps all same-module blocks, but its declaredIn map still overrides at ConfigResource granularity, so child imports for other instances are silently dropped; its unit and plan tests are solid but only exercise single-instance override.

Returns a slice like the reference, but parent-over-child overriding still works at ConfigResource granularity, so child blocks for other instances are silently discarded; unit and plan tests are reasonable but do not cover that case.

Clean recursive SectionBase computation with unnormalized handling and a good test that checks page kinds and resources; it also edits the docs, which is reasonable but outside what the task required.

A correct recursive `SectionBase` computation, with pages rebased via `CutPrefix` and resource URLs tested; it also edits the docs, which is relevant but beyond the required change, and it does not test a nested section that has its own slug.

Works via a map from segment index to slug, but adds two descriptor fields and computes a meaningless ContainerDir for branch pages (e.g. '/etiquetas' for the taxonomy); the test is decent but omits resources and slugless subsections.

It works by mapping segment index to slug and applying that to both the section base and the container dir, but the two parallel descriptor fields and the map/index arithmetic are less clean; the tests are reasonable but skip resources.

Recursive slug-aware Dir computation closely mirrors the reference design and respects DisablePathToLower; path.Join may slightly normalize odd slugs, and the solid test does not check bundle resources.

A recursive slug-aware `Dir` closely mirrors the reference: it handles nested and unslugged descendants and unnormalized paths, and the tests cover sections, nested slugs, taxonomy and term, though not bundle resources.

Replaces path segments by index for each slugged ancestor section, and checks the segment boundary when applying the new base to regular pages; it keeps the Section field and adds a fallback SectionBase, and its test covers the most ground: resources, a non-section intermediate directory, taxonomy and term pages, and unaffected English pages.

Segment-index slug substitution plus small descriptor helpers, including a path-boundary check when rebasing the container dir; the test is the most thorough, covering resources, deep slugs under a non-section dir, taxonomy, term and English pages.

Core behavior matches the spec, with very thorough tests covering unit, run, archive and cloud run. However, isOnceMode mixes detection with validation, the lower-layer shortcut handling is absent, and it changes the shared tests.Main helper with an unrelated proxy-env workaround.

Same post-consolidation transform as the reference, with conflict validation folded into isOnceMode, and the most thorough tests (unit, run, cloud run, archive); it shares the gap where lower-layer shortcuts wipe a scenario before --once applies, and it carries unrelated proxy-env changes to the test harness.

Cleanly structured in its own once.go file with separate detection, validation and transform steps, plus good integration and archive tests. It shares the same lower-layer shortcut and execution-segment gaps, and it modifies the shared tests.Main helper with an unrelated proxy-env workaround.

Correctly rewrites the consolidated options into a 1/1 shared-iterations scenario that keeps exec, env, tags and options, and rejects multiple scenarios and conflicting shortcut flags; it does not drop shortcuts from lower layers (an env/script duration or iterations still wipes the scenario before --once runs), does not reject execution-segment, and adds unrelated proxy-env test plumbing (new TestMain, change to tests.Main).

Applies the transform after consolidation and rejects conflicting CLI shortcuts correctly. It does not drop lower-layer shortcuts before merging, so an env K6_ITERATIONS can wipe the script's scenario, and it does not reject the execution-segment flags. It also adds an exported, CLI-specific helper to lib/executor, but the table and unit tests are solid and there are no unrelated changes.

Correct behaviour with no unrelated changes and good consolidation-table coverage, including the env-shortcut case; however, it puts CLI-specific logic (an exported function whose error message mentions --once) into lib/executor, which is a layering smell, and it misses the lower-layer shortcut stripping and the execution-segment conflict.

The post-consolidation rewrite works for the default, single-scenario and multi-scenario cases. It misses dropping lower-layer shortcuts and turns an unset exec into an explicit "default". It also adds unrelated proxy-env-clearing TestMain hacks in two test packages.

Works, detecting conflicts via the CLI config values after consolidation, but it ignores the GetBool error, adds an os.Exit TestMain without the lint exemption, edits tests_test.go for unrelated proxy cleanup, and misses the lower-layer shortcut and execution-segment edge cases.

Most complete: wraps literals, updates the positive and division/modulo checks, and fixes Pretty to omit unary plus like the reference, plus a prettier test; one added test locks in a dubious {0,0} error position with a FIXME comment.

Wraps parenthesised literals in both the paren and unary-paren paths, updates Pretty like the reference, and keeps the parse-time positive, division-by-zero and modulo-by-zero checks via constDurationValue; minor nits are the wrapper starting at the literal rather than the paren, no EndPos, and a FIXME left in a test.

Handles wrapping centrally (including in applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr) and updates the positive-duration and division/modulo-by-zero checks to look through wrappers, with thorough tests; it misses the Pretty unary-plus fix and uses an unchecked type assertion.

Clean approach (pre-wrap in applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr) that keeps the positive, DIV and MOD constant checks and has thorough tests, but skips the Pretty update and relies on an unconditional *NumberLiteral type assertion in paren_duration_expr.

Wrapping is safe and the positive-duration check is preserved with good error and round-trip tests, but the `ExperimentalDurationExpr` gate in the unary-paren rule is odd, division/modulo-by-`(0)` parse errors are lost, and Pretty is not updated.

Fixes the round-trip and keeps the positive-duration check with sensible paren-based start positions, but skips the Pretty update, leaves the DIV/MOD zero checks blind to (0), and gates wrapping on the experimental flag in only one of the two rules.

Wraps the bare literal in a unary-plus DurationExpr in both paren rules and keeps the positive-duration check working through the wrapper, but no longer catches division or modulo by `(0)` at parse time, leaves Pretty unchanged, and uses an unchecked `$2.(*NumberLiteral)` assertion.

Correct round-trip with accurate paren start/end positions, but uses an unconditional $2.(*NumberLiteral) assertion, skips the Pretty update, keeps only the positive check (not DIV/MOD), and adds no new error-case tests.

Structurally closest to the reference (fork-script rename of walkTemplate plus a delegating wrapper, try re-panic) and well tested, but it moves `return` into the templates namespace and silently accepts value returns in non-partials and return mid-pipeline.

Like C2 but with more careful node copying, a fork-script rename, and good tests (including try), though it moves return to another namespace, changes the store API, and silently ignores valued non-partial returns and trailing pipeline commands.

The panic-based sentinel with traps at executeWithState and walkTemplate works for early returns anywhere, but it has three gaps: a value return in a non-partial is silently ignored, `return x | y` silently drops the rest of the pipeline, and the existing regression test was weakened to match.

The panic/recover design is clean and the fork script injects the walkTemplate defer neatly, but it changes ExecuteWithContextAndKey's signature, silently drops values returned from non-partials, and silently truncates `return x | f` to `x`.

It matches the reference by erroring on value returns outside partials, but `moveReturnLast` only regroups when the second arg is a bare identifier, which breaks previously working patterns such as `return .Site.GetPage "x"` or `return $p.Param "k"`; walkTemplate is also duplicated instead of delegated.

Closest to the reference: bare returns end only the current template, a valued return in a non-partial raises the same error, and `return x | f` is rewritten so the full pipeline is returned; but it copies the upstream walkTemplate body instead of wrapping walkTemplateOld, gates on `category == CategoryPartial`, and still misses `return .Method arg`.

Early return works, but the result is plumbed through a context value and an extra state field, and exec.go is patched directly without updating the fork script, so the change would be lost on the next fork sync; non-partial value returns and pipeline misuse are also silently accepted.

Passes the return value through a context pointer and an extra state field, which is more convoluted; it edits exec.go without updating the fork script (exactly the maintenance risk the issue raises), silently drops pipeline and non-partial values, and its tests lock in an odd error message.
